newsitem.title: USA: Paula Jones case latest in long Washington saga.
newsitem.headline: Paula Jones case latest in long Washington saga.

text.p: The Paula Jones sexual harassment case that went before the Supreme Court on Monday is only the latest alleged sex saga to titillate Washington.

"Scandal is a growth industry" in the U.S. capital, said Marianne Curan, whose "Scandal Tours" visits sites of scandals present and past, with actors on the bus playing out the roles of principals. "It really keeps us busy," she told Reuters.

Now enter Paula Jones, who asked the high court on Monday to let a lower court hear her claims that in 1991, when he was Arkansas governor, Bill Clinton dropped his trousers in front of her in a Little Rock hotel and solicited oral sex.

Embarrassing stories seem to erupt before big political events in Clinton's life. Just hours before he gave his acceptance speech for renomination last summer, his top political guru, Dick Morris, was engulfed in seamy scandal.
Morris resigned that day after a newspaper publicised details of an affair he had with a $200-an-hour prostitute -- an affair that recenly led Morris's wife to leave him.
And, just as Clinton was entering the 1992 presidential primary election season, a woman named Gennifer Flowers went public with claims he had had a 12-year secret affair with her in Arkansas.
Scandals in Washington are a bipartisan matter.
One of the justices who heard the Jones case -- Republican Clarence Thomas -- was accused of sexual harassment by a former legal assistant when he was a federal official.

Those charges by Anita Hill, then a university law professor, caused a sensation during Thomas's 1991 Senate confirmation hearings. But he denied them furiously and the Senate confirmed him to to the high court bench.
Last September, Oregon Sen. Bob Packwood, another Republican, resigned his seat after the Ethics Committee recommended expulsion on a list of sexual misconduct charges.
The late John Tower, once a powerful Republican senator from Texas, was hit by a barrage of accusations of sexual affairs and drinking that sank his nomination to be U.S. defence secretary in 1989.

The presidential ambitions of the former Colorado Democratic Sen. Gary Hart were dashed in 1987 after reporters staked out a Washington town house and caught him in liaisons with a woman named Donna Rice. Hart was married.
Snickering reached a crescendo with publication of photos of Rice sitting on Hart's lap in the stern of a Miami yacht whose name, visible below, read, "Monkey Business."

One of the most spectacular scandals in modern Washington involved the late Wilbur Mills, an Arkansas Democrat and the powerful chairman of the tax-writing House of Representatives Ways and Means Committee.

The career of Mills, who was rarely seen outside of work, started crashing when police were summoned to a fracas on the Washington Tidal Basin one night in 1974. They found Mills and a woman who had leaped into the water during a late-night lovers' quarrel. She turned out to be his steady companion, a stripper stage-named "Fanne Foxe, the Argentine Firecracker."
Mills later admitted to a drinking problem and in his last years was a leading spokesman against alcoholism.

Sen. Charles Robb, a Virginia Democrat married to the late President Lyndon Johnson's daughter Lynda, survived a scandal in 1988 when he was accused of having an affair several years earlier with beauty queen Tai Collins.
While Robb denied any sexual wrongdoing, he acknowledged he did get a massage from her in a New York hotel room.

Throughout American history, there have been tales of sexual dalliance told -- eventually -- about presidents including John Kennedy, Warren Harding and even one of the Founding Fathers, Thomas Jefferson.
